hints: Focus on what these two ions actually have in common, count their electrons first.
Both $\text{S}^{2-}$ and $\text{K}^{+}$ have 18 electrons with the same argon configuration, so the difference must come from the nucleus.
Compare the number of protons pulling on those same 18 electrons and think about which nucleus pulls harder and shrinks the ion more.
walkthrough:
**Write down the electrons in each ion**

Both ions look different at first, but let's count carefully. Sulfur is atomic number 16, so $\text{S}^{2-}$ gains 2 electrons to have 18 electrons. Potassium is atomic number 19, so $\text{K}^{+}$ loses 1 electron to also have 18 electrons.

$$\text{S}^{2-} : 16 - (-2) = 18 \text{ e}^{-} \quad , \quad \text{K}^{+} : 19 - (+1) = 18 \text{ e}^{-}$$

**Spot that they are isoelectronic**

Great, so both ions have the same electron arrangement, the noble gas configuration of argon. That means shielding and number of shells are essentially the same, so they cancel out as explanations.

$$\text{S}^{2-} \text{ and } \text{K}^{+} \text{ are isoelectronic (same } 2,8,8 \text{ arrangement)}$$

**Compare nuclear charge as the deciding factor**

With the same number of electrons, size is decided by how strongly the nucleus pulls. $\text{K}^{+}$ has 19 protons pulling on 18 electrons, while $\text{S}^{2-}$ has only 16 protons pulling on 18 electrons. More protons means greater effective nuclear attraction, so the electrons are drawn in closer and the potassium ion is smaller.

options.A: This is a false general rule. Ionic radius does not always decrease with atomic number, especially when you compare cations with anions or move to a new period. Here K has higher atomic number (19) than S (16) and is smaller, but that is because of nuclear charge on isoelectronic ions, not a universal trend.
options.B: This sounds tempting but it is just a description, not an explanation. It is not always true to compare any positive ion with any negative ion, and it does not tell us why. The real reason is the difference in proton number for the same electron count.
options.C: This is correct and gives the real cause. Both ions have 18 electrons, but $\text{K}^{+}$ has 19 protons while $\text{S}^{2-}$ has only 16 protons. The greater nuclear charge in potassium pulls the same electron cloud in more strongly, making $\text{K}^{+}$ smaller than $\text{S}^{2-}$.
options.D: The charges 2- and 1+ are true facts, but on their own they do not explain size. The trap is to think charge magnitude alone decides radius. What matters is the balance of protons to electrons: 19 protons vs 18 electrons for $\text{K}^{+}$ compared to 16 protons vs 18 electrons for $\text{S}^{2-}$.
